summary: Astro Team: Lunar South Pole Landing Site Navigator is an interactive, browser-based 3D educational and exploration tool designed to help students, educators, and space enthusiasts understand the engineering challenges of landing at the lunar south pole. Using real NASA elevation maps, shadow-free surface imagery, and orbital data, the platform simulates how the low polar Sun casts long shadows across craters and how direct communication with Earth changes over a 30-day timeline or at custom lunar coordinates. Instead of requiring complex specialist software, users can explore a 3D lunar globe, filter viable landing zones, and inspect individual craters in an interactive diorama mode with simplified visual indicators alongside deeper telemetry. By turning raw NASA planetary data into a clear visual experience, Astro Team makes the science behind Artemis and future lunar exploration accessible to everyone.
details:
What It Does and How It Works

Astro Team: Lunar South Pole Landing Site Navigator is an interactive, browser-based 3D platform that allows users to explore landing candidates at the lunar south pole across a 30-day timeline from November 15 to December 15, 2026, as well as any custom lunar coordinates. The experience follows a three-stage guided flow. First, the Landing Overview introduces the Artemis south pole exploration challenge. Second, the Global Explorer displays an interactive 3D Moon where users adjust a UTC time slider and viability filters, such as minimum illumination percentage and maximum terrain slope, to highlight suitable regions. Third, the Local Diorama Mode isolates a high-resolution 3D terrain cutout of a selected site where real-time directional sunlight, dynamic crater shadows, a direct-to-Earth communication vector, and toggleable scientific layers for topography, thermal permanently shadowed regions, and orbital telemetry respond smoothly at 60 FPS.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Scientific tools like NASA Quickmap or JPL Horizons are built for specialist analysis and require interpreting raw numerical tables across separate interfaces. Astro Team bridges that gap with an accessible, educational approach. It includes two user profiles. Level 1 translates complex orbital mechanics into intuitive visual indicators for students, educators, and the general public, while Level 2 exposes detailed engineering metrics including solar and Earth azimuth and elevation, partial and full-disc visibility, round-trip communication latency, and sunrise and sunset countdowns. Because it runs directly in any standard web browser without specialized software or accounts, it helps classrooms and space enthusiasts grasp why polar topography makes solar power and Earth visibility so challenging for Artemis and CLPS missions.

Tools, Languages, and Technologies Used

For the data and orbital engine, we used Python with FastAPI, Skyfield, NumPy, SciPy, and OpenCV alongside GDAL to process LRO LOLA digital elevation models, extract 360-degree terrain horizon profiles, remove embedded shadows from LROC WAC imagery via homomorphic filtering, and compute planetary ephemerides with JPL DE421 and IAU lunar orientation models. For the frontend and 3D visualization, we used Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Three.js with React Three Fiber, implementing custom GLSL shaders for terrain isolation and real-time shadow casting. For infrastructure and storage, we used Supabase PostgreSQL for site catalogs and hourly timelines, static JSON caching, and Vercel for web deployment.

Creativity and Key Design Factors

Rather than presenting a traditional flat map, Astro Team models each lunar crater as a physical-style 3D terrain diorama mounted on a matte pedestal with stacked holographic data layers. Watching long shadows sweep across a crater floor as the time slider moves makes the polar illumination problem immediately intuitive. Key factors considered by the team included maintaining vertex-to-vertex alignment across all South Polar Stereographic maps, preserving lossless 8-bit elevation data to avoid false terrain terraces, and ensuring smooth performance on standard laptops by caching timelines in browser memory.
